lessons.title: Metals and Mining: Global Prices, China, and the Commodity Cycle

body.text: A metal company does not set the price of what it sells. A tonne of aluminium is the same whether it comes from Odisha or Oman, so the price is set on global exchanges and by what is happening in China. The only things an Indian metal company controls are its cost per tonne, its volumes, and its debt. That is why analysing metals means analysing the spread, not the sales.

children.text: Tata Steel, JSW Steel, Hindalco Industries, Vedanta, Hindustan Zinc, SAIL, and Jindal Steel are among the most heavily traded stocks in India, and they are also among the most misunderstood. Chapter 2 introduced them as the most cyclical part of the market, with the deepest P/E traps. This lesson explains what actually drives their earnings and how to value them without being fooled by a record year.

columns.label: A metal company (price taker)
points: Sells a standardised product at prices set globally, on exchanges like the LME or by import parity
Cannot raise prices without losing all its customers
Competes on cost per tonne and reliability of supply
Earnings swing with prices it does not control

columns.label: An FMCG company (price maker)
points: Sells a branded product customers ask for by name
Can raise prices and keep most of its customers
Competes on brand, distribution, and product
Earnings are far steadier through the cycle

children.text: The Only Metric That Matters: EBITDA per Tonne

Because a metal company sells a measurable physical product, analysts strip everything down to two numbers: how many tonnes it sold and how much operating profit it made on each tonne. Management commentary, analyst questions, and quarterly presentations all revolve around EBITDA per tonne, realisation per tonne, and cost per tonne. Learn to think in these units and metals results become much easier to read.

body.latex: \text{EBITDA per tonne} = \text{Realisation per tonne} - \text{Cost per tonne} \qquad \text{Total EBITDA} = \text{EBITDA per tonne} \times \text{Tonnes sold}
body.caption: The spread is the business. Volumes multiply it.

stats.label: Cost
stats.context: Iron ore, coking coal, power, conversion, freight

body.title: What a 10% Price Fall Does
body.prompt: Using the illustrative steel company above, global steel prices fall 10%, so realisation drops from ₹55,000 to ₹49,500 a tonne. Costs stay at ₹45,000 a tonne and volumes are unchanged at 20 million tonnes. What is its new total EBITDA, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: New EBITDA per tonne = ₹49,500 - ₹45,000 = ₹4,500. Total EBITDA = ₹4,500 × 2 crore tonnes = ₹9,000 crore, down from ₹20,000 crore. A 10% fall in the selling price cut operating profit by 55%. This is operating leverage from Chapter 2 in its most extreme form: when costs are largely fixed in the short run, the entire price move lands on the spread.

body.text: Reverse the maths and you see why metal stocks can multiply in a boom. If realisation rises 10% instead, EBITDA per tonne goes from ₹10,000 to ₹15,500 and total EBITDA rises 55%. Add debt, and net profit moves even more. Metals are a leveraged bet on a price you cannot forecast.

children.text: Cost per Tonne: Where Companies Actually Differ

markDefs.definition: Owning the mines that supply your own raw material, such as iron ore or coal, instead of buying it from the market. Captive supply lowers cost and protects margins when input prices spike.

children.text: Since everyone sells at roughly the same price, the winner is whoever produces most cheaply. The single biggest factor is

. A steel company with its own iron ore mines is far less exposed when ore prices spike than one buying everything. The second is energy: aluminium smelting in particular consumes enormous amounts of electricity, so captive power plants and access to coal matter hugely. The third is downstream value addition, where converting metal into higher-value products earns a processing margin that is steadier than the raw commodity price.

body.caption: What Decides Cost Position in Indian Metals

cells: Insulates from raw material price spikes
Share of requirement met from own mines, disclosed in annual reports
Largest bought-in cost for steel; power cost for aluminium
Import dependence, captive coal blocks, linkage coal from Coal India
Share of power generated in-house and fuel cost
Processing margins are steadier than commodity prices
Share of value-added products in the sales mix
Spreads fixed costs and lowers conversion cost
Capacity utilisation and conversion cost per tonne
Freight to ports and customers is a real cost per tonne
Distance from mines, ports, and demand centres

children.text: Why China Decides Your Steel Stock's Quarter

China produces and consumes roughly half the world's steel and is the dominant buyer of many other metals. When Chinese construction and property demand is strong, Chinese mills absorb their own output and global prices firm up. When Chinese property slows, those mills keep running and export the surplus, pushing prices down across Asia. Because Indian steel prices are set close to import parity, cheap imports quickly cap what Indian mills can charge, even when Indian demand is healthy.

body.title: How a slowdown in Chinese property reaches an Indian steel mill

events.title: Chinese construction slows
events.description: Property developers build less, so Chinese demand for steel falls.

events.title: Mills keep producing
events.description: Large steel plants cannot be switched off cheaply, and employment matters locally, so output stays high while domestic demand falls.

events.title: Surplus is exported
events.description: Chinese steel is offered across Asia at low prices, pulling regional benchmark prices down.

events.title: Import parity caps Indian prices
events.description: Indian buyers can source cheaper imported steel, so domestic mills must match or lose volume. Realisation per tonne falls.

events.title: Policy responds
events.description: Domestic producers seek protection, and the government may impose safeguard or anti-dumping duties on imports, which can lift domestic prices again. Government action cuts both ways: export duties have also been used to cool domestic prices.

body.title: Read the Metal News Flow
body.question: Which headline is most likely to lift the earnings of an Indian aluminium producer?
options: The rupee strengthens sharply against the dollar
LME aluminium prices rise and domestic coal supply improves, lowering power costs
The government reduces import duties on aluminium products
A major domestic competitor announces a large capacity expansion
body.explanation: Higher metal prices widen realisation while cheaper power lowers cost per tonne, expanding the spread from both sides. A stronger rupee reduces rupee realisation for a dollar-linked commodity, lower import duties increase competition from imports, and new domestic capacity adds future supply that can weigh on prices.

children.text: The Capex Trap and the Debt Problem

Metal companies make the most money at the top of the cycle, which is exactly when they feel confident enough to announce large new plants. Those plants take three to five years to build and often start producing into a weaker market, adding supply when prices are already falling. Worse, expansions are usually part-funded with debt, so the company carries higher interest costs into the downturn. This combination, high operating leverage plus high financial leverage, is what turned India's steel and power expansion boom of 2008 to 2014 into the bad loan crisis you studied in Chapter 3.

body.text: For metal stocks, always check net debt to EBITDA using normalised EBITDA, not peak EBITDA. A company at 1.5 times peak EBITDA can be at 4 or 5 times mid-cycle EBITDA, which is where lenders start worrying and equity holders get hurt.

body.title: The Expansion Announcement
body.scenario: A steel producer has just reported its best year ever: EBITDA per tonne at a record, net debt to EBITDA down to 1.2 times, and a higher dividend. It announces a ₹40,000 crore expansion to add 8 million tonnes of capacity over four years, part-funded by debt. Brokerages raise target prices, citing strong cash flows and volume growth ahead. Two other Indian producers have announced expansions in the same quarter, and Chinese exports are rising.
body.prompt: How would you assess this announcement?
body.modelAnswer: Treat the current year's numbers as peak, not normal. Record EBITDA per tonne means the spread is unusually wide, so net debt to EBITDA of 1.2 times is flattered; recalculate it using a mid-cycle spread, where it could easily be two or three times higher. The expansion itself is not necessarily wrong, since India's steel demand is growing and low-cost capacity can be valuable, but the timing and the industry context matter: multiple domestic expansions plus rising Chinese exports point to more supply arriving into a softer price environment, which is how commodity cycles usually turn. Questions to ask: What is the capital cost per tonne compared with peers and with buying existing assets? Is the project backed by captive raw material that will keep it low on the cost curve? What does the balance sheet look like if prices fall 20% during construction? Is the dividend sustainable alongside the capex? Will the company slow spending if prices fall? The best cyclical managements expand when assets are cheap and others are retreating, not when everyone announces at once.

children.text: P/E is nearly useless here, for the reasons you saw in Chapter 2. Analysts use EV/EBITDA on normalised or mid-cycle EBITDA, price to book, and a check that is specific to commodities: enterprise value per tonne of capacity. If a company's enterprise value per tonne is far below the cost of building a new plant, the market is pricing the assets below replacement cost, which has historically been a useful signal near cycle bottoms. If it is far above, the market is paying today for capacity that does not yet exist.

body.title: Enterprise Value per Tonne
body.prompt: A steel company has an enterprise value of ₹1,20,000 crore and installed capacity of 20 million tonnes a year. What is its enterprise value per tonne of capacity, in rupees?
body.explanation: 20 million tonnes is 2 crore tonnes. ₹1,20,000 crore ÷ 2 crore tonnes = ₹60,000 per tonne. Compare this with what it costs to build new steel capacity today. If a new plant costs meaningfully more per tonne, the market is valuing existing assets below replacement cost. If building is cheaper, existing capacity is richly valued, and new supply is likely to arrive.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Because metal companies sell a standardised product at globally set prices, the key profitability metric analysts track is EBITDA per ___.
body.explanation: EBITDA per tonne isolates the spread between realisation and cost, which is what actually drives a metal company's earnings.

body.title: Analysing a Metals and Mining Company
steps: Find realisation per tonne, cost per tonne, and EBITDA per tonne for the last eight quarters
Compare the current spread with its own history to judge where in the cycle you are
Check raw material integration: captive iron ore, bauxite, coal, and captive power as a share of requirement
Note the share of value-added and downstream products, which earn steadier processing margins
Track the global benchmark price and Chinese production, exports, and property activity
Check net debt to EBITDA using mid-cycle EBITDA, and the size and funding of any announced capex
Value using EV/EBITDA on normalised earnings, price to book, and enterprise value per tonne of capacity, not reported P/E

points: Metal companies are price takers; prices are set globally, so earnings depend on the spread between realisation and cost per tonne
EBITDA per tonne is the core metric, and a small price move produces a much larger profit move
Cost position is what separates companies: captive raw materials, captive power, scale, value-added mix, and logistics
China produces and consumes roughly half the world's steel, so Chinese demand and exports drive global and Indian prices through import parity
Government action cuts both ways, with export duties used to cool domestic prices and safeguard or anti-dumping duties used to protect producers
Expansions announced at the top of the cycle add supply and debt into a weaker market, which is how cyclical booms turn into balance sheet problems
Value metals on normalised EBITDA, price to book, and enterprise value per tonne, never on peak-year P/E

body.text: All realisation, cost, capacity, and valuation figures in this lesson are illustrative and do not represent any specific company. China's share of global steel is approximate. Company names are examples, not recommendations to buy or sell any security.
